chapters.summary: Chair Julie Won welcomes attendees to the oversight hearing on the Office of Community Hiring and recognizes Council Members Hanif and Epstein.
chapters.title: Chair Julie Won opens hearing and recognizes colleagues

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome to today's oversight hearing of the Committee on Workforce Development.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: My name is Julie Wan and I have the privilege of chairing this committee.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Before we begin, I'd like to recognize my colleagues who have joined us, Councilmember Hanif and Councilmember Epstein.

chapters.summary: Won describes community hiring as using city contracts to hire low-income New Yorkers, NYCHA residents, and residents of high-poverty neighborhoods. She notes 2023 state authorization, January 2025 rules, and an initial projection of 36,000 jobs annually.
chapters.title: Chair explains community hiring program and projected jobs

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Today we're looking at the Office of Community Hiring.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The idea behind community hiring is simple.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The city spends billions of dollars each year on contracts and the companies and nonprofits that get awarded those contracts should be hiring New Yorkers who need the work.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: In 2023, Albany gave the city the power to set hiring goals on city contracts for low-income New Yorkers, NITRA residents, and people living in our highest poverty neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The city's own rules took effect in January 2025.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: When the program launched,

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The administration projected 36,000 jobs a year once it was fully up and running.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: In February, New York City Talent told this committee that more than 200 procurements were already out on the street and that program could reach upwards of $20 billion in city contracts each year.

chapters.summary: Won says OCH's latest quarterly report shows 179 contracts worth about $3 billion with hiring goals, up from 60 contracts worth $1 billion. She highlights low progress on construction and service contracts, implausible percentages, and missing required data on hires, pay, and demographics.
chapters.title: Chair reviews OCH reports and data gaps

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: But then we started looking at the Office of Community Hiring's own reports.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: OCH's latest quarterly...

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: report was posted just last week and it shows 179 contracts worth about $3 billion carrying a community hiring goal up to up from 60 contracts worth about $1 billion in March.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: That's real growth, but unfortunately the progress hasn't kept up.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Of the 83 construction contracts, only 8 reported any progress and 6 of these 8 were below the 30%

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: community hiring goal.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: On all five contracts from the apprenticeship goal that reported progress, the share of hours worked by apprentices from these communities was zero.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: For service contracts, 94 contracts now carry community hiring goals that add up to more than 3,000 hires, but more than half of them still have no progress reported at all.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And some of the numbers that are reported don't add up.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: One Department of Social Services Workforce Development Program in Queens has a goal of 31 hires, but OCH's report shows it at more than 1,200% of that goal.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Either something remarkable is happening or OCH is counting something other than new hires.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And nowhere in these reports does the city say how many people have actually been hired.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The law requires these reports to show how many people were hired, what they're paid, and who they are, and that information still isn't in there.

chapters.summary: Won questions whether OCH has enough staff to follow up on reporting, asks what happened to the first $1.2 billion security and fire safety procurement, and warns against repeating Hire NYC's pending referrals. She states the hearing goals: real hire counts, a publication date for required data, and a vendor accountability plan.
chapters.title: Chair raises staffing, first procurement, and Hire NYC history

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So today I want to understand what's behind these numbers, where nothing has been reported, has the work already started, and vendors just aren't reporting, or is it that OCH doesn't have the staff or the systems to follow up?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: In February, New York City Talent told us,

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: that it has 37 staff in total.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I want to know how many of them are working on community hiring and whether that's enough to keep up with the program that's nearly triple in size in a single quarter.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I also want to know what happened to the program's very first procurement.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: In June 2024, the city announced $1.2 billion in procurement for security guard and fire safety services as its first community hiring effort, and the city expected those contracts to be placed by 2025.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: They still don't appear in any of OCH's reports.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: This isn't the city's first try at this.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Back in 2019, under Hire New York City, about 80% of job referrals were marked as pending for years because employers never told the city whether anyone was hired.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: We can't afford to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What we'll be looking for today is a real count of how many New Yorkers have been hired through community hiring, a date for when the city will publish the data the law requires, and a plan for holding vendors accountable when they don't meet their goals.

chapters.summary: Douglas Harry, Executive Director of NYC Talent, introduces himself and G. Lee, Executive Director of the Office of Community Hiring, and thanks the committee for the invitation.
chapters.title: Douglas Harry introduces himself and G. Lee

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Juan and members of the New York City Council Committee on Workforce Development.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: My name is Douglas Harry, and I'm the Executive Director of the New York City Office of Talent and Workforce Development, or NYC Talent.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I'm joined today by G.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Lee, Executive Director of NYC Talent's Office of Community Hiring, or OCH.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Thank you for inviting us to testify today.

chapters.summary: Harry describes NYC Talent's mission to connect New Yorkers to good jobs and employers to local talent, noting the public workforce ecosystem includes over 120 programs across nearly 30 agencies.
chapters.title: NYC Talent mission and workforce ecosystem

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: NYC Talent's mission is to ensure that the city's workforce system connects New Yorkers to good jobs and helps employers access local talent.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Our public workforce ecosystem includes more than 120 programs administered by nearly 30 city agencies,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: including the Department of Small Business Services, the Human Resources Administration, the Department of Youth and Community Development, the City University of New York, and New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: While each agency focuses on its own core mission, NYC Talent works across these partners to align the city's workforce strategy with job seeker needs, employer demand, and a changing economy.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Community hiring exemplifies NYC Talent's efforts to design and launch interagency initiatives to deliver a better workforce system.

chapters.summary: Harry explains community hiring as a first-of-its-kind program embedding equity into city contracting. It applies to construction, human services, standard services, and professional services, and OCH manages rollout, support, and reporting.
chapters.title: Community hiring program overview and scope

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Community hiring is a first-of-its-kind program in the nation that aims to embed equity and opportunity into city contracting.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: New York City's local government has many city agencies that provide a wide range of services for New Yorkers, from designing parks and playgrounds to providing health care and child care to repairing roads and bridges.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: While some of this work is done by city employees, the city also contracts with vendors, which include businesses and nonprofits, to deliver billions of dollars in services every year.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Community hiring allows the city to leverage its purchasing power by setting workforce goals on these contracts for vendors to hire low-income individuals and residents of low-income communities, including NYCHA housing.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Community hiring was authorized by state legislation in 2023, and NYC Talent was tasked with transforming the framework established in the law into an operational program that has a tangible impact on New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: While there are similar programs in other cities and states that are generally limited to the construction industry, the city's program goes further and applies to a broad range of contracts, including construction,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: human services like healthcare, standard services like cleaning and moving, and professional services like technology and engineering.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: OCH manages the rollout and implementation of the program, supports city agencies and vendors, and reports on progress toward community hiring goals.

chapters.summary: Harry reports 528 contracts with community hiring goals representing $13.3 billion in value, and approximately 1,200 community hires employed by vendors to date, though most contracts are early in their terms.
chapters.title: Program results: 528 contracts, $13.3B, 1,200 hires

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We are proud to share that, as a result of these efforts, 528 contracts have community hiring goals, which represents $13.3 billion in contract value.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Despite most of these contracts being recently registered and early on in their contract term,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We already have approximately 1,200 community hires employed by vendors to date.

chapters.summary: Harry describes the formal rulemaking process after the 2023 state law, including engagement with 120 external partners and 47 city agencies. The community hiring rules took effect January 23, 2025.
chapters.title: Rulemaking and stakeholder engagement

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I want to take this opportunity to walk you through the work that has made these accomplishments possible.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: After the state legislation that authorized community hiring was signed by the governor in November 2023, we were required to complete the city's formal rulemaking process to establish the operational framework for the program.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: This included determining details about what type of contracts are covered, how city agencies set goals, and what vendors need to do to comply with goals.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: OCH worked collaboratively while developing these rules so they would be informed by the perspectives of the many stakeholders impacted by community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: OCH heard from 120 unique external partners through one-on-one meetings, information sessions, roundtables, and panel discussions.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: These groups included organized labor, elected officials, workforce development organizations, industry groups, pre-apprenticeship programs, human service providers, and community organizations.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: OCH also engaged with 47 different city agencies and offices through one-on-one meetings and bi-weekly agency working groups.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: After this process, the community hiring rules went into effect January 23, 2025.

chapters.summary: Harry says 2025 focused on training city agency staff to set goals on applicable contracts. OCH reviewed Passport procurements, held about 200 meetings, trained over 115 staff from 27 agencies, and completed a phased rollout by September 2025.
chapters.title: Agency training and phased rollout

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Since community hiring is tied to city contracting, our major priority in 2025 was ensuring that city agency staff were aware, trained, and prepared to set goals on their agency's applicable contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We reviewed contract information from Passport, monitored procurements being released by agencies, and held approximately 200 meetings with city agency procurement staff to discuss opportunities to set goals.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We held training sessions that were attended by over 115 city agency staff.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: representing 27 agencies, developed an agency-specific FAQ document, and created standard contract language.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: After a phased rollout, by September 2025, we had supported all mayoral agencies to ensure they were prepared to implement community hiring across their applicable contracts.

chapters.summary: Harry describes vendor preparation through FAQs, procurement events, and 77 pre-solicitation conferences. OCH established a referral source network of 81 organizations, including unions, Workforce One centers, HRA Business Link, and community-based organizations.
chapters.title: Vendor outreach and referral source network

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We also focused on preparing city vendors so that they had the information they needed to understand, comply with, and benefit from community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: These efforts included publishing a vendor-specific FAQ document on our website, attending community and procurement events to conduct vendor outreach, and presenting during pre-solicitation conferences to provide guidance to vendors interested in responding to solicitations for procurements with goals.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: To date, we have presented at 77 pre-solicitation conferences.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: To help vendors fill their workforce needs and meet their community hiring goals, we established a network of referral sources, which are entities authorized by our office to connect vendors with qualified job seekers in search of opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We intentionally designed our referral source network to drive more employers and more jobs to the public workforce system.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Currently, our network includes 81 organizations, including labor unions, SPS's Workforce One Career Centers, HRA's Business Link, and dozens of community-based organizations that have contracts with agencies like DYCD for job placement services.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Referral sources conduct outreach to their communities.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Provide free job placement and recruitment services, determine job seekers are eligible as community hires, and help ensure that candidates meet a vendor's employment needs.

chapters.summary: Harry says accountability is embedded through quarterly reports on contracts and vendor progress. OCH has published nine quarterly reports but is still building digital infrastructure for data tracking.
chapters.title: Accountability, reporting, and digital infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Accountability.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: is embedded into the design of community hiring, as we are required to publish quarterly reports on contracts subject to community hiring goals.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: These reports include aggregate and vendor-specific progress towards goals and information about placements and demographics of community hires.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Regular reporting will not only increase transparency, but will also provide a long-term opportunity for the city to continuously improve the program by identifying opportunities for targeted outreach,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: where training programs could be developed to better align the skills of job seekers with the needs of city vendors.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: While we are still building some of the necessary digital infrastructure, we have published nine quarterly reports to date, all of which can be found on our website, nyc.gov slash community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Under the leadership of Mayor Mumdani and Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice, Truly Sue, we are committed to strengthening the workforce system as essential public infrastructure to connect New Yorkers to opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Community hiring is an important tool that strategically leverages city contracts to drive employers and jobs to the public workforce system, while also improving interconnectivity across city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Vendors and programs so that job seekers and businesses mutually benefit.

chapters.summary: Harry notes city procurement is complicated and embedding community hiring requires digital systems, labor partnerships, and stakeholder preparation. He says progress is significant but more work remains, and he is ready for questions.
chapters.title: Procurement complexity and closing

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I know firsthand from working many years at the Mayor's Office of Contract Services that city procurement is an extremely complicated process that offers immense opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Embedding community hiring into this process

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: developing multiple digital systems for data tracking and analysis, strengthening collaborations with our partners in organized labor through project labor agreements, and preparing numerous disparate stakeholders for program implementation has been an enormous effort.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I'm incredibly proud of the progress we have made to date.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But no, we still have a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We look forward to answering your questions and discussing how we can work together to realize the full vision of community hiring and connect more New Yorkers to quality employment opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Thank you, and we are happy to take your questions.

utterances.text: So we started in terms of growing our referral source network with starting with the public workforce system, and that's SBS, who operates the Workforce One Center, HRA's business link team, which also does

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: job connection services, particularly for...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: who are receiving public benefits.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But we've also expanded to the city agencies who are contracting with nonprofit providers for this work.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so many of the providers now are

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: have contracts with DYCD, but we also have NYCHA and their REIS program.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We're looking to expand for CUNY as well as other city contracted vendors.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so in terms of the process for identifying, we work with the city agencies and we're continuing to work with the CBOs of making sure they are plugged in and authorized to

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: become referral sources.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Our goal is to have as much expansive connection across all of the city, all the populations.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We're proud that there are referral sources in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so the process is really trying to maximize the amount of opportunities for New Yorkers through these referral sources.

utterances.text: I would encourage you to reach out to us.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, I mean, you know, Councilman Juan, she knows the groups in her district.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I can tell you I don't hear Henry Street, Grand Street Settlement, Asian Americans for Equality.

utterances.text: University Settlement.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: These are settlement houses just to operate in my district that have a big, wide, you know, swath of contact to people.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They have, like I mentioned, we have a lower side employment network.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We have the Jobs Plus training program.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So we have things that exist, there's structures that exist that I think would be really helpful.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So if you reach out to our offices, you can get that information.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And you can reach out to our comms people and be like, hey, put this in your e-blast so people know that we exist.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We want to be able to reach out to people.

chapters.summary: Epstein describes a veteran in his district who has been job searching for six months and did not know about community hiring. He says poor communication is a problem. Harry agrees to work with the Council to expand outreach.
chapters.title: Epstein shares veteran story and communication issues

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We all get calls.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I get calls every day.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I got a call the other day from a veteran in my district.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: He's like, I've been looking for six months to try to find a job.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This is someone who's served our country, lives in my district, and can't find a job.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: A perfect person who's got a great track record working in nonprofits.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: To be able to be in this cohort, they don't know that it exists because the poor communication up to date.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We're happy to work with you, Council member, and the whole Council to really expand some of the outreach and awareness.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Some of the organizations you mentioned, we do as an office have relationships with Lesson and Henry Street, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And like I said, where we are right now today, we're at the list that I shared, but I do anticipate that that will continue to grow over the coming weeks.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so happy to have that partnership and have you help amplify that messaging, both for the CBO community as well.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how many employment opportunities OCH expects over the next three years. Harry says goals are driven by city procurement and will vary, noting $13 billion in registered contracts and 528 contracts.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about expected employment opportunities

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How many employment opportunities do you expect to be available over the next three years that are going to be flowing through you?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So that's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: All of the job opportunities and the goals are driven by city procurement.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so it depends exactly on how much an agency or the city agencies covered by this are procuring each year.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so it will vary over time depending on what the procurement looks like.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But we are excited that we have already $13 billion worth of city contracts registered to date.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It's 528 contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so the types of organizations that are getting those contracts vary.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so their hiring needs may vary, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Like every contract doesn't necessarily necessitate hiring a certain amount of people.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But we are continuing to look at the data and collect that information and work with the vendors to see how the city can help best.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks how many potential jobs are available across the 528 contracts. Harry says he does not have that exact number and that OCH is beginning to work with vendors to identify opportunities.
chapters.title: Epstein asks how many jobs in 528 contracts

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So in these 585 contracts, how many potential jobs are there available?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Right now, I don't have that exact number of potential jobs available.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Many of these contracts, like I said, the data that we published in our most recent report was only at 179 because that was based on the quarter that we were mandated to publish.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Since then, we're already at 528, so a lot of new contracts have just been registered.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We have yet to do exactly the analysis that you're looking for in terms of what the

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: that those job opportunities are, but we are now beginning to work with those vendors to make sure that they are working with the system, working with referral sources to help identify what those job opportunities may be.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: When can you get us the information about how many jobs for the 528 contracts you have might be available to New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We'll work on getting that information to you as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We'll have to go back and see where all of those contracts are in the particular status and what some of the outreaches look like to date from our partners, but we will be able to get it.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks for a two-week update on available contracts and job types, saying real data will help the Council understand whether the program is creating 5,000 jobs or five. Harry agrees to follow up in two weeks.
chapters.title: Epstein asks for two-week update

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Is that like two weeks, three weeks, six months, a year and a half?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I don't think it'll be a year and a half, Councilmember, but I do think it really depends on where these contracts are.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can you just give us an update in two weeks to say, this is the information we have to date.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: These are the contracts that we have available.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This is what we know so far.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: These are the types of jobs we're seeing available.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Because I think the real data is going to help us.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I mean, I don't want to speak for the chair, but I think...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If it's 5,000 jobs versus five jobs, it's a very different conversation.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If it's 5,000 jobs in a variety of industries, it's a very different conversation about our role and how we can be helpful.

chapters.summary: Epstein says knowing job types and industries will help nonprofits and training programs prepare workers. Harry notes many contracts are multi-year and vendors may not know all hiring needs on day one.
chapters.title: Epstein stresses data for training

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I think what we're trying to do is say we want this to work, we want it to be successful, but we want to make sure that you're doing the appropriate outreach.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So the people I talk to get it.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many times I hear from people like, the city did this hiring hall for jobs.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I went.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: The line was out the door.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I waited for three hours, never met with anybody, and I left.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: That level of frustration I hear is a problem that we're not right-sizing what we're trying to do, and this is a way to try to right-size it to help people.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Happy to follow up in two weeks with what we have as of then and welcome the continued conversation.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I do also want to note that because of the nature of the contracts, and many of them are multi-year contracts, even the vendors might not know all of their hiring needs on day one of the contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But that's why we're working with them continuously to try to assess that.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But happy to follow up and continue to partner on.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks that the follow-up include the types of expertise and positions needed. Harry says community hiring covers entry-level and professional jobs across construction, human services, standard services, and professional services.
chapters.title: Epstein asks for contract/job type list

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Can I just, Chair, can I just one more question?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So when you send us the list of 528 contracts and the potential jobs available and the potential areas where these jobs might be, it would be great to know what expertise we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Because if there's in these contracts the same type of positions we're looking for,

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: That will send a message.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You mentioned, you know, lesson.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: That will send a message to lesson, be like, oh, we know these type A, waking up something, these hotel jobs are really coming down the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We see a lot of these jobs.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We should be educating and training people to be ready for these jobs.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: as we move forward.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So when we're doing job retraining, this is something important for us.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: This kind of data, since you're saying that most of these are multi-year contracts, will be really helpful for the nonprofits we partner with to be able to help assess what they need to be doing in training and education.

chapters.summary: Epstein thanks Harry and Chair Won for the time. Won thanks Epstein.
chapters.title: Epstein thanks; Chair thanks

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And one of the things that we're particularly excited about with community hiring, which, as I mentioned, is unique here in New York City, is that it's not limited to only entry-level jobs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It's not limited just to construction, which these types of programs typically are.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It's the professional services jobs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It's the human services jobs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It's the standard services jobs and construction.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we're excited about the diversity of different types of job opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And we'll continue to work with all of our vendors and our referral sources to make sure that we are getting that information out there.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for the time.

chapters.summary: Won asks whether recruiters at Jobs NYC hiring halls are recruiting for community hiring, how someone inquiring about community hiring is served, and about staffing and hours. She cites complaints about long lines and poor follow-up.
chapters.title: Chair asks about Jobs NYC Center and hiring halls

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And I want to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmember Kavan.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: On September 28, 2026, DCAS and SBS opened a Jobs NYC Center at 2nd Lafayette Street in Lower Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: While the mayor was praised for converting a long, empty building into a space for career services and workforce development, multiple attendees have cited that event was poorly organized, leaving many job seekers scrawled in the process, as Councilmember Epstein has described.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Are recruiters at these halls recruiting individuals for community hiring needs?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And if someone walks into a hiring hall inquiring about a community hiring opportunity, how are they being serviced?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Can you help me understand how many staff are on site at all times?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What are the hours?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What is going on?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because I get so many complaints as well where we've seen it in the news where over, I think over 50,000 people have applied to jobs to the city of New York and they haven't even heard back at all and they're really upset.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And I think a single digit was hired into this new administration's agencies.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So there's just so much confusion and so much frustration if you could help us understand better.

chapters.summary: Harry says the new Jobs NYC Center focuses on city jobs, while community hiring is for non-city contracted vendors. He says SBS staffs the site and can route people to Workforce One services.
chapters.title: Harry explains Jobs NYC Center focus and SBS routing

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I think I lost it.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So specifically as it relates to community hiring, that new Jobs NYC Center is focused primarily on city jobs, and the nature of community hiring is non-city jobs because these are city contracted vendors.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so in terms of community hiring direct services happening at that site, it's not designed to do that.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: However, SBS, who is staffing that site, and we're happy to work with you, council member, or get that information back from SBS in terms of the details on how many people there, the exact hours, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But again, that is geared towards city jobs, whereas community hiring is non-city jobs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: However, because it is...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Run by SBS, then they operate the Workforce One system.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: For people who are entering, looking for job opportunities, I believe SBS is able to help route them to back through the Workforce One Center and then

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: make sure that the job opportunities or training opportunities that people might be interested in, whether it's city or not, they can get connected to those services as well.

chapters.summary: Won asks how the administration separates NYC Talent, the Office of Community Hiring, and SBS in workforce development. Harry explains OCH is part of NYC Talent, which works across city partners including SBS.
chapters.title: Chair asks about separation of offices

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Can you help me understand how this administration separates Office of Talent and Workforce Development versus community hiring versus SPS on who's doing what workforce development?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Like, how are you guys deciding?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Who's covering what scope?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because for me, I think workforce development covers all of this.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So our office, the Office of Talent and Workforce Development, the Office of Community Hiring, I recognize it's confusing to have an office within an office, but the Office of Community Hiring is part of NYC Talent.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so the work around community hiring, everything that I've shared in my testimony and here

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: today is part of NYC Talent.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: NYC Talent generally works across all of the city partners who are doing workforce development, and that includes SBS.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so like the Workforce One centers that SBS operates are run by SBS, staffed by SBS through SBS contracts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And we at Talent work closely with SBS and the many partners.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: For community hiring specifically, while it's run out of our office, the intention and design behind community hiring is really

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: to bring more jobs, to bring more employers, to bring better jobs, the diversity of jobs into the public workforce system.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And that, again, based on our referral source network, right, we want to make sure that HRA, SPS, DYCD, the many CBOs, labor unions are all plugged in to help connect job seekers to these opportunities.

chapters.summary: Won asks how OCH checks whether contractors on project labor agreements follow the agreement's referral process, not just the 30% hiring goal. Harry says OCH monitors progress through certified payroll reports and works with building trades.
chapters.title: Chair asks about PLA referral process

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: On construction contracts covered by a project labor agreement, how does OCH check whether contractors follow the agreement's referral process, not just whether they reach the 30% hiring goal?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So for any contract subject to goals, we and the contracting agencies, we're monitoring the progress towards the goals.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so for PLAs specifically, our city PLAs right now have a goal of 30% directly in those PLAs, the way the state legislation is written.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It requires us to follow what that goal is in the PLA.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we will monitor.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: The progress towards the goals like any construction project.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That's through collecting digital certified payroll reports and the data that is on those certified payroll reports to track towards the goal.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We have a really strong partner with the building trades and they're committed to doing community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We're excited that it's embedded directly into our PLAs.

chapters.summary: Won asks what results PLA-covered construction contracts have shown. Harry says 23.75% of all hours have been performed by community hires based on available data.
chapters.title: Chair asks results for PLA construction

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And so far, what has been the result for construction contracts covered by PLEs?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So based on the data we have now, let me see if I can get the specifics.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: the goals to date.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Well, so I do have the, I was able to get to your earlier question, the percentage of hours.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So right now, 23.75% of all the hours have been performed by community hires.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That's based on the available data that we have now.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We're continuing to collect more data about these contracts as these contracts progress and as we get more contracts registered.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I can see if we have that broken down by PLA and non-PLA contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but generally across all of the construction contracts, it's about 23.75% of hours worked have been performed by community hires.

chapters.summary: Won asks OCH to differentiate PLA and non-PLA tracking, and asks who decides whether a PLA contractor made best efforts and what happens next. Harry says OCH works with agencies and vendors on a bespoke best-efforts process.
chapters.title: Chair asks about PLA differentiation and best efforts

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: If your team can also check how they're differentiating and tracking the metric for PLAs, that would be really helpful.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And if a PLA-covered contractor falls short, who decides whether it made its best efforts and what happens next?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Like who's doing the regulations and standardization checks for quality control on these contracts?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Yeah, so our office works with the contracting agencies to help assess the progress towards the goals and compliance with the goals.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Like you mentioned, it is a best efforts based program.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so best efforts will vary depending on the type of vendor who is doing the work, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It is not a one size fits all, you know.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Big mega corp might have more resources and their best efforts might be a little different than mom and pop Inc.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we will work closely with the agencies.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We will work with the vendors.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: to make sure that they are making best efforts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And that will be working with, and say on PLA contracts, working with labor, working with the city's public workforce system to try to make sure that community hires are connected to these job opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But again, it's somewhat of a bespoke process that allows for us to take into account

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: the specifics of the types of organizations who are holding these contracts.

chapters.summary: Won yields to Council Member Phil Wong. Wong asks how OCH identifies contracts with community hiring goals and what it does to reach contracts without goals.
chapters.title: Chair yields to Wong; Wong asks how contracts are identified

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, and I'm also going to pass it over to Councilmember Wong for questions.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chip.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This is my data over here.

utterances.text: As of July 2026, 179 registered city contracts worth about $2.96 billion carry community hiring goals.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question to you is, how do you identify city contracts?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That carry community hiring goals and what are you doing to reach out to the other contracts that do not have these hiring goals?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because 179 contracts is a very small figure compared to all the contracts I've seen

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: in like an open data or passport?

chapters.title: Harry explains applicability and contract value

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So many of the contracts that we have to date, they're just newly registered.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so because we're early on in this process, we anticipate that our, or we know rather that that contract count will continue to grow.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: For example,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Between that last report, which has 179, we already actually now have a total of 528 contracts registered.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: They just haven't been yet reflected in the report, and that's valued at $13.3 billion.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: In terms of applicability,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Much of the applicability and structure around community hiring is rooted in state law, and so it applies to all service contracts, and there are some exceptions, but generally that's construction services, professional services, standard services.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: and human services.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So it's like all services excluding goods contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so our rules that we put into place, and like I said in the testimony, the rules were shaped by many, many different stakeholders, external and internal, of putting the structure of rules into place.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Generally speaking, it is all services contracts valued at $3 million or more, with some exceptions.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And some of those exceptions, like I said, are in state law.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Right now, in that report, there were just 179.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It will grow in the next report to 528 once we publish that data.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But generally speaking, in terms of the types of contracts that get procured every year by the city agencies,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We think almost like 90% of the contract value of services contracts that get procured every year will be covered by community hiring once all of those contracts go through the full procurement cycle and cycle through.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so whereas the contract count is one piece, the contract value is the piece that we're most focused on because, you know.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Five contracts that are only a million dollars is going to be less than one contract that's 50 million dollars for example and so we think that uh the vast vast majority of services contracts that get procured by city agencies

chapters.summary: Wong asks what outreach is done to high school and college graduates who do not go to college, saying he had never heard of the Office of Community Hiring before today.
chapters.title: Wong asks about outreach to youth and college grads

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: will be covered by community hiring thank you um my follow-up questions regarding uh

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: outreach because you take any person, grad

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: graduated from college or from high school that decides not to go to college.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How are you, what kind of outreach are you doing to let them know, here you can work for these city vendors and here are the ways to get hold of them?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What exactly is being done?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like, I've never heard of until today, New York City Talents Office of Community Hiring.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: This is total news to me, and I can tell you that a lot of community-based organizations in my district would certainly want to reach out to you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Either they need looking for talent or they want to be part of this community hiring process.

chapters.summary: Harry says most outreach is through the referral source network. He cites a September 30 HRA community hiring job fair with 25 employers, 388 job seekers, and 16 conditional offers.
chapters.title: Harry details outreach and September 30 job fair

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we've done outreach ourselves through our office to a variety of vendors and community partners as well.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: However, most of the outreach and connection is done through our referral source network, through the city agencies who operate the Workforce One Center, SBS, and HRA, who does its business link, and the CBO providers.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: By design, we want to drive more people to the workforce system, and community hiring is designed to do just that, increase the amount of employers that are partnering with the workforce system, increasing the amount of jobs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: From a job seeker perspective, we obviously want them to know about that community hiring is here and that there's an opportunity for more jobs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: jobs coming through.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But at the end of the day, we really just want to make sure that people are being connected to the workforce system and that those CBOs are able to provide them with

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: whatever services they may need, which may be a community hiring job, but it may be a different job that is not necessarily directly tied to community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so with that being said,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We do have some, we do partner with our partner agencies.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: On September 30th, we actually had a partnership with HRA for community hiring job fair.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We had 25 employers who participated in that, 388 job seekers, and there were even 16 on-the-job conditional offers made.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we're happy to partner with you, Councilmember, on increasing the outreach and having more events just like that.

chapters.summary: Wong invites OCH to hold a job fair in his district. Chair Won thanks Wong.
chapters.title: Wong invites job fair to district; Chair thanks

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Come to my district and do a job fair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I would love it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Won asks about a PACE contract in Queens with a goal of 31 hires showing 1,229% progress and an ACS contract showing 18.67%. She asks what the figures represent and whether they are typos.
chapters.title: Chair asks about PACE contract 1,229% and ACS contract

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: 13 of the contracts that were held by the Department of Social Services for the Pathways to Access Careers and Employment and Wellness Comprehensive Assessment, Rehabilitation and Employment, so PACE and We Care programs,

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: which provide employment services to cash assistant clients.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: In OCH's fourth quarter report, a PACE contract in Queens with a goal of 31 hires shows the progress of 1,229%

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: and an ACS non-secured detention contract with a goal of 12 shows 18.67%.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What do these figures represent?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How many people were actually hired under this contract?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And is that a typo?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because the math ain't mathin'.

chapters.summary: Won asks Harry to quantify the 1,229% figure. Harry says the vendor is exceeding its goal because goals are formula-based and hiring needs vary; he does not have exact math on the spot.
chapters.title: Chair asks to quantify; Harry says exceeding goal

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So the goals are based on the contract value for those types of contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And we did confirm those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: They are just hiring many, many people.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we're proud that those vendors have been able to help.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So can you quantify many, many, many?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What is many, many, many that it comes out to be?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I forget the...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I don't have the exact math, and forgive me, I can't do the math on the spot right here.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: However, across all of the contracts, you have about 1,200 community hires employed to date.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: For those contracts, the non-construction contracts, it's a little over 1,100.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: If 31.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Was the goal on that?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: You know, maybe a couple hundred folks have been hired on that, but don't quote me on the exact math there.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, because the contract amount is $15,685,874, and the hiring goal was 31, and the community hiring goal percentage progress is 1,229%.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: They are exceeding their goal.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And that's because they just have, based on the, and again, the way that community hiring works is we set the goal based on a formula, essentially.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But we know that the way that employers hire is not necessarily rooted based on some contract value formula.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It's rooted on based on their needs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So that employer had a higher need.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We're glad they were able to work with the public workforce system to hire community hires for those jobs.

chapters.summary: Won asks whether vendors self-report or OCH inspects and collects data. Harry says construction uses digital certified payroll reports, while non-construction data comes from referral sources and vendors, with a digital tool being implemented.
chapters.title: Chair asks about reporting process

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So for all these contracts, what is the process for reporting?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Are they self-reporting back to you, or are you going and inspecting and collecting data?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How is this working?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we are early on in the process of having these contracts, but we are able to collect this information digitally, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so on construction contracts, we have a digital tool that contractors on construction are required to submit certified payroll reports.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That's state law.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We've digitized that process, and we are collecting information from those certified payroll reports, and we are able to use that information in addition to tracking all of the prevailing wage requirements and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: to track community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We are still ramping up the implementation of this tool, and so we anticipate that more and more contracts will be using it, will increase our reporting for community hiring as well.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That's on the construction side.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: For the non-construction contracts, there's a couple different ways that we're able to collect that information.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We can work and are working directly with the referral sources who have that data.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And sharing it with us, we are able to collect information directly from the vendors themselves.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And we are also in the process of implementing a digital tool to collect that information and share information across the various agencies to streamline some of the data collection and reporting to try to minimize

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: the burden on vendors, on our referral sources and agency partners.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That process is underway and putting into that digital tool so we can collect that information and report.

chapters.summary: Won asks how OCH collects non-construction data before the digital tool is in place. Harry says it is a mix of information from referral sources and vendors, with verification through referral sources.
chapters.title: Chair asks how data collected now

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So as that tool is coming into play for non-construction contracts, how are you collecting the data now that you've shared with us?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So that's been a mix of information collected directly from referral sources, as well as I think we have some information that we've been able to collect directly from

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: vendors as well based on their reporting and telling us we work with so-and-so referral source.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: In those instances, we would work with the referral source to verify that information.

chapters.summary: Won asks what happens to vendors that fail to report. Harry says there is a penalty mechanism under the law and rules, but OCH prefers to work with employers first and can assess financial penalties for failure to make best efforts.
chapters.title: Chair asks about accountability penalties

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And for accountability for those who have failed to provide the reporting, what happens to those vendors?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Yeah, so there is a penalty mechanism under the law.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: and under our rules.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: With that being said, for true success of this program, we want to make sure that we are working with these employers and helping meet their needs and really so understanding what are their hiring needs and are they actually working with the public workforce system?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Are they working with referral sources?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Are they publishing these jobs and making them available and accessible to New Yorkers?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So that's core to it.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: If in the case where vendors are failing to do that and failing to make best efforts, there is the ability for the city to assess financial penalties on these vendors for failing to do that.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Intend to use that if we need to, but for many of these contracts, they're pretty early on in their process.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so while we're monitoring on a constant basis, we know that hiring needs are not necessarily driven directly by the contract term.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we're not at the point yet where we have to do that, but we are prepared to do that if we need to.

chapters.summary: Won asks how the penalty is calculated and whether it is a percentage of contract sum. Harry says he will share the rules and contract language, noting the penalty can scale with severity and lack of participation.
chapters.title: Chair asks penalty amount

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And for the penalty, is it a percentage of the contract sum?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What is the penalty amount?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And how is it calculated?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That's a good question.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I'll have to share.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We can share the rules and the contract language for that exact amount.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But it is a, there's a certain dollar amount and it can scale up depending on the severity and the value and the lack of participation by the vendor.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We don't want it to just be a cost of doing business, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We want it to make sure that people are...

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: This all sounds good.

chapters.summary: Won asks whether the former administration's projection of 36,000 jobs annually is still accurate and when full implementation is expected. Harry says the projection was based on estimated procurement spend and labor market analysis, and OCH is continuing to assess hiring needs.
chapters.title: Chair asks about 36,000 jobs projection

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I look forward to the new system for non-construction contracts for reporting.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: In June 2024, the former administration projected that the community hiring would create an estimate of 36,000 jobs annually once fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Is this projection still accurate?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: When does OCH expect the program to be fully implemented?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And how does OCH measure the program to meet those projection goals of 36,000 jobs annually and that you are on track?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Yeah, so this number at the time was analyzed based on a variety of estimated procurement spend, budget documents, labor market analysis.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So it was reflective of what the program may be when it's fully, fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: All contracts that could have community hiring have community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: They're actually fully going through the full procurement cycle, which means not just the procuring of that, but the actual service term, right, so the many, many years.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That projection was made many years ago.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We are continuing to look at procurement spend and what is in the procurement pipeline, and most importantly, working with the vendors and really understanding the hiring needs, because we do know that hiring is not exclusively based on what a contract amount.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: As you mentioned, Chair, there is one vendor who has an exceptionally high hiring need, and they were able to dramatically exceed their goal, which is great, but it makes it a little tough to estimate the exact amount.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But we are very excited that even with the one

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: 79 contracts that were registered to date and published in the report that's hit nearly 1,200 community hires so far.

chapters.summary: Won asks how OCH aligns community hiring requirements with actual employer demand, especially in healthcare. Harry says goals are formula-based for ease of administration and NYC Talent has industry partnerships, including in healthcare.
chapters.title: Chair asks about health department classification and employer demand

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The health department is the largest service agency in all the program, yet health-related jobs and community hiring reporting framework are displayed under

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Human Committee on Workforce Development Services.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: On human services, professional services, or other classifications depending on what the city purchases.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What does OCH determine whether community hiring requirements are aligned with actual employer demand?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And given significant workforce needs in healthcare and other essential industries, what is the city's strategy for ensuring these sectors benefit from community hiring?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So for all of the contracts that are subject to community hiring, the way that goals are set, and this is for largely ease of administration,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: both for agencies and vendors, it's a formula-based, right, which not necessarily, as I said, tracks exactly to hiring needs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so for services that the city is procuring, we're excited that we're able to drive more of those employers to the workforce system and get them to continue to.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Bring jobs to the system, bring higher quality jobs to the system, and help meet the needs of

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: those employers, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: With that being said, we know that these are not

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: the only employers and so that are working in within the city and are hiring from the system and so community hiring is part of that and we're able to bring more of those employers but there are needs beyond

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: just city contracted providers and so the city does a lot of work to help connect New Yorkers to all of those opportunities and we're always looking at

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: even separate just from our community hiring team, but we have industry partnerships that work, specifically one that works in healthcare.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we're looking at data, both what are hiring trends, what are hiring needs today, what are the hiring needs tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so that's something that is a focus of our office to make sure that we are

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: working with our agency partners to build a workforce system that is both responsive to the needs today of employers, but also the needs of the employers in the future.

chapters.summary: Won asks where contractors have the greatest difficulty meeting hiring goals and what barriers exist. Harry says it is early and OCH does not yet have sector-specific analysis but will use data to inform training.
chapters.title: Chair asks where contractors have difficulty

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Where are contractors having the greatest difficulty meeting hiring goals and why?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And are there barriers related to available vacancies, required credentials, candidate preparation, recruitment process?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Practices or contracting funding and what is OCH doing to address them?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So because we are early on and many of these contractors still recently registered, we don't have all of the answers to that exactly, but we will continue to work with the providers to, or rather the employers, to understand what their hiring needs are, where

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: there are challenges and where they think that they might not be meeting their goals.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And if that's because of something that the city needs to improve upon, we'll use that data to inform how we are making sure that, say, we are increasing training opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we will continue to monitor that, but I don't have quite the sector-specific analysis on that yet.

chapters.summary: Won notes public shortages of social workers and nurses and asks about city partnerships with CUNY to help people finish education. Harry says NYC Talent focuses on apprenticeships and increasing opportunities beyond community hiring.
chapters.title: Chair asks about social workers/nurses and CUNY

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, because it's been public in the news how we're short in social workers and nurses, especially in the health care sector.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So are there any efforts from the city of New York in partnership with CUNYs to make sure that there are programs to allow people to finish their education, especially since the federal government has declassified them as public servants?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Yeah, so that is something that, like I said, beyond community hiring that our office is always focused on of trying to increase opportunities, help make sure that we are connecting more New Yorkers and improving job quality and things like that through apprenticeships.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so that is something that we are focused on.

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: The fiscal year 2027 adopted budget includes a budget of $1.7 million and 16 positions for OCH, with $388,200 being for contractual services.

utterances.text: Are there any key positions that have been difficult to fill?

utterances.text: And I would also love to hear from OCH's executive director, G.

utterances.text: I'll let you speak to the staffing of the OCH team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So the Office of Community Hiring is currently a team of eight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: We have one civic court member and one intern.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And are there any key positions that have been difficult to fill?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Is there any vacancy?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Because we're supposed to have 16 positions, and you're saying that there's eight.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So are you vacant for six positions?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I mean, for more than six positions?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So the 1.7 million was for 16 positions within OCH.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: You have eight people.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: That means that you have vacancy of 50%.

utterances.text: So we have some of our headcount is actually at other agencies that are supporting the community hiring initiative.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we have, because by design, we want to make sure that this actually, this work is embedded into the state system.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So there are two.

utterances.text: Community hiring headcount that are really staffed most directly at SBS who help support community hiring, but they are

utterances.text: So they are not part of that eight they are part of our headcount but are in doing the work in support of community hiring and again that is intentional because we want to make sure that this is not a side effort this is embedded into the

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: the public workforce system.

utterances.text: So we do have other vacancies at the moment.

utterances.text: Okay, so you have six vacancies.

utterances.text: I think we have, I'm not sure exactly which data year, but we right now have a total of three vacancies on the community hiring budget.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, so we'll have to follow up because the adopted budget has a $1.7 million

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: allotment or allocation for OCH and it's for 16 positions.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Happy to follow up with the data that we have and make sure it's all up to date.

utterances.text: Okay, so the vacancies that you have that you believe are three, which we have at six, they don't have titles?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Right now, we are continuing to look at what those needs may be in terms of the system.
