utterances.text: Okay, so they're not even job openings.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Right now, we do not have active postings on the community hiring side.

chapters.summary: Won asks whether additional positions or funding would help OCH reach the 36,000 jobs goal. Harry says OCH would never say no to resources but is excited about digital tools reducing person-power needs.
chapters.title: Chair asks if additional positions help

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And do you believe that additional positions or funding can help OCH reach the goal better of 36,000 jobs created annually?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We would never say no to additional resources, but we're really excited about the progress we've been able to make to date.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And like I said, with our digital tools, we're really trying to maximize the ability for us to use, collect data digitally, which will reduce the person power to make sure that we have a good and successful program.

chapters.summary: Won asks how many and what type of contracts the $388,200 set-aside supports. G. Lee says OCH is investing in technology to implement, scale, and track the program, with broader workforce system benefits.
chapters.title: Chair asks about $388,200 contractual services

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, and out of the $1.7 million, there's a set-aside of $388,200 for contractual services in the OCH budget.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How many and what type of contracts does this funding support?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So our office is investing in technology to effectively and efficiently implement, scale, and track the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So these investments are not only going to support community hiring, but the data that we're able to collect will really be used for a broader impact across the workforce system.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So the entire $388,200 goes to one technology budget or contract?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: We're trying to look at it for all different types of technology.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How many tech contracts are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: There's nothing currently in the works, but we're working through that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, so the money is unspent.

chapters.summary: Won asks whether the money is unspent and whether it goes to one technology contract. Harry says some money is under contract for a consultant helping with technical implementation; G. Lee identifies the firm as JK Consultant.
chapters.title: Chair asks about consulting firm

utterances.text: We have some money under contract for...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: consultant who is helping on some of the technical implementation.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So they're not a tech contractor per se.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So it's an individual LLC, not a firm.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Like a freelancer?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: It's a consulting firm.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It's a consulting firm.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Which firm?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: JK consultant.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Won notes the city charter requires quarterly reports to include demographics, compensation, total hires by contract type, and financial benefits, but OCH reports lack this. Harry says OCH will publish more data and gives preliminary borough breakdowns for human services hires.
chapters.title: Chair asks about missing demographic/compensation data

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And the city charter requires each quarterly report to include the demographic and compensation of community hires, the total number of community hires by contract type, and the program's financial benefits.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: None of the information appears in OCH's published reports.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Why has OCH not published this information, and when will you begin publishing it?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So in the most recent reports, we don't have some of that information, but we do have some of that information that we hope to reflect in the future reports.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And we will continue to collect this information as we implement those tools to make sure that we have it.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But we do know that we have community hires from all five boroughs, neighborhoods across the city from Harlem to Stapleton and Staten Island to East New York to Corona.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we're hiring, we know, from across all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We know that specifically on human services contracts, approximately 27.5% are from the Bronx, 36.5% are from Brooklyn, 12% are from Manhattan, and 22% are from Queens, and 1.5% are from Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And that's based on the available preliminary data now.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: know that we want to continue to make sure that we are collecting this information, being mindful of privacy and sensitivity of collecting and publishing data.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we will continue to collect that information and be able to publish it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: When will it be published?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We will publish the data as soon as

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We're able, in accordance with the reports, as we have the data based on those contracts, we will publish the data.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we will continue to improve what those information that is in those reports to make sure that we are getting all the information that we can have.

chapters.summary: Won asks OCH to share demographic breakdowns internally with the Council. Harry agrees to provide the data and contextualize it relative to the quarterly reports.
chapters.title: Chair asks to share internally

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Can you at least share it internally to the council so that we understand the demographic breakdown?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We're happy to provide you, Chair, with the data that we have so far and contextualize it with what that is relative to the reports.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But again, because of the way that the quarterly reports are, it's always a little bit behind from when that quarter of what we're publishing to what we actually do.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so since...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That last report, we still have more data that we've been collecting.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so some of that information that we've been able to do has just yet to meet or be reflected in those reports, but happy to share that with you.

chapters.summary: Won notes the fourth quarter FY2026 report still does not state the number of people hired. Harry says OCH has about 1,200 hires to date and will ensure reports include required information.
chapters.title: Chair asks why number hired missing

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, and OCH's fourth quarter report for fiscal year 2026 was posted this past week, and it still does not state the number of people hired.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Why is that statistic always missing?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So, like I mentioned, we do have about 1,200 hires to date.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Not sure exactly of what the data point, but.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: in terms of what specific is in the reports and what you're referencing, but we're happy to share that information with you and make sure that our reports have all the information that is required.

chapters.summary: Won says 94 service contracts carry about 3,150 income-based hire goals, and 53 show no progress. She asks whether no hires were made or just not reported. Harry says it is likely a mix of recent contracts, future hiring needs, and incomplete data collection.
chapters.title: Chair asks about 94 service contracts, 53 no progress

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: As of June 30th this year, 94 service contracts carried combined goals of about 3,150 income-based community hires.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: 53 of them showed no progress data at all.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Does that mean no community hires have been made under those contracts or they have just not been reported?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And how...

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Well, you already answered this question of how the vendors on service contracts report the hires to OCH.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So can you just answer, has there been no community hiring under those contracts or have they just not been reported?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So this is for the 94 service contracts carried combined goals of 3,150 income-based community hires and 53 of them do not show any progress.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So I...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I don't know the exact details of all 94 of those.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: However, I'll say that it's a mix of both probably, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Because some of the contracts are very, very recently registered.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: They might be multi-year, maybe as long as like five-year contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so all of their hiring needs may just not happen yet, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: They might not have a hiring need today, but they might have a hiring need tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: In some cases, we just might not have collected all of that information from them just yet.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: As I said, we're early on in trying to capture all of that information.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we will continue to work with those providers.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so it will run the gamut in terms of how they're...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I guess it could be either or in that case or both.

chapters.summary: Won notes only eight of 83 construction contracts reported progress, and six were below the 30% goal. She asks what OCH and DDC have done. Harry says many contracts are incomplete and hiring needs vary by project stage.
chapters.title: Chair asks about construction contracts below goal

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: In OCH's most recent quarterly report, only eight of the 83 construction contracts reported any progress.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Six of those eight were below the 30% community hiring goal.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What have OCH and DDC done about the contracts below the goal, and how many of the other construction contracts have begun their work?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So I don't have all of the information of exactly where each of these contracts are.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Many of these contracts are not complete right now, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so the hiring needs are different and the goals are different.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And especially in the construction trades, it's different types of job opportunities that might be on the project later in the project versus earlier, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: You're not painting the building until after you build it kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we will continue to work with the agencies, work with those vendors, and work with our partners in labor for PLA contracts to make sure that we are meeting hiring goals.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Because it was very early on, we are heartened to see that there is progress already towards those goals based on the data that we've been able to have.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And we will continue to monitor those contracts and work to make sure that the vendors are meeting their goals or making best efforts at least.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Won says all five contracts with apprenticeship goals that reported progress showed zero hours by community hire apprentices against a 9% goal. Harry says apprenticeships are important but it is early and OCH expects more apprentices.
chapters.title: Chair asks about apprenticeship hours zero

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: All five contracts with an apprenticeship goal that have reported progress showed no hours worked by apprentices who are community hires against the 9% goal.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Why are no community hire apprentices working on these contracts?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So apprenticeships is really...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: An important part of the work that we do in the community hiring team, but even beyond.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We believe that the apprenticeships are a really good tool for talent development because they're paid on-the-job training.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So far, we don't have data on any apprentices working today.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But again, since we're early on, we do anticipate that we will continue to see and get more apprentices who are community hires working on these projects.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Like I said, we have a really strong partnership with the building trades and through our PLAs, and so we're always looking for good ways to get more New Yorkers into the trades, working as apprentices and advancing to journey person.

chapters.summary: Won asks how many of the 700 pre-apprenticeship positions announced in November 2025 have been filled and how community hiring contributes to the 30,000 apprenticeships by 2030 goal. Harry says he does not have the data but will follow up.
chapters.title: Chair asks about 700 pre-apprenticeship positions

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: In November 2025, the city announced an agreement with the building trades to fill 700 pre-apprenticeship positions with residents of NYCHA housing and low-income communities.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How many of these positions have been filled, and how many community hiring contributes to the city's goal of connecting 30,000 New Yorkers to apprenticeships by 2030?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I don't have the data on the specific pre-apprenticeship numbers, but happy to get back to you based on the information we're able to collect.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But that is something that we are definitely excited about, connecting more New Yorkers and getting them into the trades through the pre-apprenticeship programs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So we'll follow up.

chapters.summary: Won asks how OCH decides whether a vendor made best efforts, who decides, and how it is reviewed. Harry says the framework comes from state law and is not one-size-fits-all; OCH looks for meaningful participation with the workforce system.
chapters.title: Chair asks about best efforts definition

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Under OCH's rules, a vendor that misses the community hiring goal is not out of compliance if it shows that it's made best efforts to find community hires.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: A vendor that does not demonstrate best efforts can receive a notice of noncompliance on a penalty of $2,500 plus $1,000 per week for failing to take required corrective action.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How does OCH decide whether a vendor has made a best effort?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Who makes the decision and how is it?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: reviewed and can you define best effort because we've seen this in contracting over and over again with bad actors and the vague language of best effort is extremely hard to define

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: yeah so the best efforts framework is rooted in the state legislation and so that language specifically comes from the state law

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: With that being said, one of the things that is unique to community hiring, which is not common across many types of structures, is our ability to actually assess penalties.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And as I mentioned earlier, the best efforts analysis is somewhat unique depending on the type of vendor, because vendors who have more resources have the ability to actually do more in terms of making best efforts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It's not a one-size-fits-all, and we will continue to work with the vendors to make sure that those who are not meeting their goals are actually working with the Workforce One system,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: posting their jobs publicly, meaningfully participating in events like hiring events and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so there's not just like a check-the-box thing.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: If you do this, this, and that, you'll make best efforts, and that's by design, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We want to make sure that vendors are meaningfully actually participating in.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: The system.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And as you mentioned, the penalty framework does allow for, there's a penalty that allows to scale over time.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So if people are continually to flog the rules and not make best efforts and not work with us, the penalties can actually grow to quite a large amount.

chapters.summary: Won asks whether any agency has issued a notice of noncompliance or assessed a penalty under community hiring rules. Harry says not yet to date.
chapters.title: Chair asks if any notice of noncompliance

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Has agency issued a notice of noncompliance under the community hiring rules yet?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And if so, how many and which agencies?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And has any penalty been assessed?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Not yet, not to date.

chapters.summary: Won asks how a vendor's community hiring record will be considered in future contract awards. Harry says failure to meet goals or make best efforts can be reflected in performance evaluations and future contract considerations.
chapters.title: Chair asks about performance evaluations

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How will a vendor's community hiring record be considered in performance evaluations on future contract awards?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Yeah, so...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Hello?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm just testing my mic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: Sorry, guys.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It works.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So the performance of, sorry, lost my train of thought.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: The ability to meet the goals will be considered in a performance evaluation like many of the other factors, and it can be considered.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So if a vendor fails to meet their goals, fails to make best efforts, and is assessed penalties, those are the types of things that would definitely be considered in a performance evaluation and would be part of

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: their future contract as agencies consider performance evaluation and look at things like cautions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It will, if the vendor fails to do that, that will be reflected in their performance evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We would work with the agencies to make sure that those types of noncompliances are reflected in performance evaluations and any necessary disclosures, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And then that information is always considered by contract or by agencies in any future contract award.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we do take seriously the compliance piece of this and wanting to make sure that people are meaningfully participating and trying to meet the community.

chapters.summary: Won notes NYC Talent previously said over 200 procurements were on the street and the program could reach $20 billion annually. She asks how many solicitations with goals have been released and awarded. Harry says 528 registered contracts worth $13.3 billion and 362 procurements worth $18.4 billion released.
chapters.title: Chair asks about solicitations released/awarded

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, in February, New York City Talent testified that you all were over 200 procurements out already on the street, and that the program could reach upwards of $20 billion a year.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: As of June 30th, registered contracts with community hiring goals totaled $2 billion.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How many solicitations with community hiring goals have been released to date and how many have been awarded?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So I can give you the number on registered contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And right now, and this was actually as of last week, so it probably went up a little bit, but we had 528 registered contracts for a total value of $13.3 billion.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so as you know, Chair, the procurement process is not always like...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Exactly the same across every single agency and it varies.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so while the last reporting cycle had the data that we published in that one, we've since seen a spike of contracts that have been registered in this last quarter.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we anticipate, or we know that the next publication, the numbers will go up quite a bit in terms of registered contracts and registered

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: contract value.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: In total, right now in terms of procurements, in procurement we have 362 procurements that have been released valued at $18.4 billion so far.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And again, that's reflective of our initial phased rollout and ramping up these contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we're excited that that's a lot of

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: which means there's a lot of vendors and more job opportunities getting driven to the system.

chapters.summary: Won asks which agencies have released procurements with community hiring goals and which have not. Harry says the last report had 14 agencies, and the next report will show nearly all mayoral agencies, upwards of 20.
chapters.title: Chair asks which agencies

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And which agencies have released procurement with community hiring goals and which agencies have not?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So I know that I have the data from our last quarterly report, and so that has 14 agencies from DDC, who has the most, down to some of the smaller agencies with fewer contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But data that is not yet reflected in our report for the last quarter, but will be in the next one once we publish it, we have nearly all mayoral agencies.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: I think there's upwards of 20 different agencies that have contract goals subject to community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And again, that's not necessarily reflective of anything other than

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: the types of procurements that agencies are doing, the volume, does it meet the requirements, and the time in which that contract is procured and registered.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we're excited that all of the agency, our agency partners are working with us to make sure that they are setting goals appropriately and releasing contracts subject to goals.

chapters.summary: Won asks whether OCH has approved CBOs as referral sources and whether it plans a solicitation to expand the network. Harry says OCH has 28 CBOs and is continuing to work with agency partners to expand.
chapters.title: Chair asks about referral sources and solicitation to expand

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: OCH's referral source director names two referral sources, SBS's Workforce One, Career Centers, and HRA's Business Link, along with several union referral systems.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Has OCH approved any community-based organizations or other, yeah, you shared the community-based organizations.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And other workforce providers as referral sources?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And does OCH plan to issue a solicitation to expand the network?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And if so,

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we do, like I mentioned earlier and read through the list of the 28 CBOs, we do, because we are early on in the implementation, we're continuing to work with our agency partners to make sure that the CBOs, and like I said earlier, we're really

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: happy to work with the council to make sure that we are getting more CBOs plugged into this.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we look forward to continuing to expand opportunities for more CBOs to connect with community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we're happy to continue to collaborate on that.

chapters.summary: Won asks how OCH tracks referral outcomes. Harry says OCH is putting digital infrastructure in place to streamline coordination and track referrals from CBOs and agencies.
chapters.title: Chair asks tracking referrals

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And how does OCH track the outcomes of these referrals?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What is your tracking system for referrals?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So as I mentioned, the same system that we are trying to, or that we are rather putting into place and working to implement in terms of collecting information is what we hope to use to help better track referrals and information that is coming from

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: the various CBOs and agencies that are doing it.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we're putting the digital infrastructure into place to really try to streamline the coordination and interagency

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: working and connecting with all of the CBOs because there are many CBOs and many players, and we want to make sure that it is a streamlined process of trying to use technology where we can.

chapters.summary: Won says OCH declined to lower the income threshold for income-based community hires from 300% to 150% of federal poverty guidelines. She asks whether that remains the case. Harry says the 300% threshold was based on feedback from CBO and agency partners.
chapters.title: Chair asks about income threshold 300% vs 150%

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, this one is very disappointing to me.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: When adopting the rules, OCH declined to lower the income threshold for income-based community hires from 300% to 150% of the federal.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: poverty guidelines stating that referral sources may prioritize lower income job seekers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So does that remain the case in practice?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we did have the ability to set the specific threshold for what meets an income-based community hire.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That decision was not made by us alone.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We worked very closely with many agency partners, many CBOs, to get to a place that we thought was appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so 300% was the one that we were hearing the most amount of feedback and recommendations that we do that because it allows CBOs and the city workforce system to continue to serve.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Um,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: the lowest income, but also people who are just getting 200, 300%, also being able to serve those who had expanded the pool a bit, and intentionally so.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And that was based on feedback, largely from our CBO partners, as also our agency partners who are serving these populations.

chapters.summary: Won initially apologizes, then clarifies that 300% of the poverty line means higher income than 150%. Harry confirms 300% expands the population to higher incomes, and Won retracts her apology.
chapters.title: Chair clarifies 300% means higher income

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Also, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I misunderstood, because I'm thinking about AMIs.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: So 300% poverty line means that you're actually hiring people with lower income than 150%, correct?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So the range is anyone who is up to 300% of the federal poverty threshold.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so I forget what the exact income is, the dollar amount.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And it varies, obviously, depending on household size.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But it is expanded.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we're able to still hire people who are only at 100% or 150 or 250.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: But 300% means that they are even lower income, correct?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It would mean that they are higher income.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So they're at 300% of the federal poverty level.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So I think it's about...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: A single household would be like an income of $47,000, $48,000.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And how much is $150,000?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: It would be about half of that.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we've expanded the population with the 300%.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, so then my initial understanding was correct, that 300% below the poverty line means that they have a higher income.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Higher income, correct.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, so I take it back.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I retract my apology.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Understood.

chapters.summary: Harry says the 300% threshold was not decided independently; OCH worked with HRA and CBO partners to continue serving low-income populations. He notes many of the 1,200 hires are on public assistance.
chapters.title: Harry explains decision with HRA

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: As I mentioned, Chair, that was a decision that we did not independently just decide upon.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We work closely with our agency partners, particularly at HRA, who are serving a low-income population.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And we want to make sure that they can continue to serve that low-income population.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We know that of the many 1,200.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: New Yorkers that many of them are on public assistance, which also just in terms of the definition are lower than that 300% level.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so while it is a little higher, it was intentionally so based on feedback from our CBO partners and agency partners.

chapters.summary: Won notes NYC Talent previously testified to 37 staff and asks how many work on community hiring. Harry says the core team is eight, with additional data, external, and operational support.
chapters.title: Chair asks how many of 37 staff work on community hiring

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: In February?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Of this year, New York City Talent testified that it

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: We had 37 staff and three apprentices and a fiscal year 27 program budget of approximately $2.7 million.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How many of your 37 staff work on community hiring?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Yeah, so I mentioned that we have, or my colleague mentioned the team of eight right now, but we do have other staff, like particularly around data, that help support the reporting and data collection.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we, there's the core staff of a team of,

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: eight right now, but we also have other staff that help support both from the data side, some of the external side, and some of the general operational side.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so our office, you know, community hiring is one of the real core initiatives of our office, and so there's a lot of support, but it's a core team that supports it as well.

chapters.summary: Won asks what has been completed and what remains in integrating community hiring into procurement and digitizing reporting. Harry says OCH has gone from zero to 528 contracts and 1,200 hires, and is digitizing construction payroll and building broader data systems.
chapters.title: Chair asks about integration/digitization progress

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: OCH's November 2024 instructor report described work to integrate community hiring into the city's procurement and workforce systems and to digitize paper-based reporting.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What has been completed so far and what remains to be done?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So I don't want to rehash all my testimony, but we really are proud of the work that has been done to date.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: This went from zero contracts, zero anything, and no rules whatsoever, to now we have over 528 contracts already registered, estimating at $13.3 billion worth of contracts.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we're incredibly proud of that work that has been done to date, the 1,200 hires based on only that one at 79 contracts that have been published in our reports.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And we've already begun digitizing a lot of this process, particularly on the construction side, trying to transform a paper-based process into collecting information digitally.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And we are continuing to work to put the...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Digital technology in place to really better collect data, share data across agencies.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so there's definitely more work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: We're still early on in this process, and this is not a subtle effort, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: This is a really big systems change for all the city agencies doing procurement.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so proud of the work to date, but certainly more.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: More work ahead of us.

chapters.summary: Won asks what average salary a community hire can expect. Harry says jobs vary widely across construction, human services, standard services, and professional services, and many are prevailing wage or union jobs.
chapters.title: Chair asks average salary

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: What is the average salary one can expect from a community hiring opportunity?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So the types of jobs that are through community hiring are quite varied because it applies to such a broad range of different types of contracts from construction to the human services to standard services to professional services.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So it really depends on the type of job and the hiring needs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But we know that many of these jobs are prevailing wage jobs, good union jobs in many cases.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so we are excited about those opportunities and making sure that we are driving more jobs to the workforce system.

chapters.summary: Won asks G. Lee what her top operational priority is and what results to expect next quarter. G. Lee says her priority is building program infrastructure, including digital systems, vendor outreach, and strengthening the referral source network.
chapters.title: Chair asks G. Lee top priority and next report

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: For OCH Executive Director Lee, since becoming Executive Director, what have you made your top operational priority and what updated results should this committee expect to see in the next quarterly report?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for your question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So my priority for our team is to continue building out the infrastructure of our program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: That includes, as Executive Director Lepar mentioned, finalizing and putting into place digital systems to improve data collection, tracking of community hiring goals,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: Additionally, we want to broaden our vendor outreach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: As we've heard today, we see the importance and we recognize the importance of continuing to meet with our stakeholders and see how we can better support the job seekers across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: Additionally, we also want to strengthen our referral source network.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: We recognize that they're key players to making community hiring a success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So we are thinking through how to build out that structure to ensure that we're not just

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: growing the number of referral sources for referral sources sake, but just really thinking through how we can all work together and not compete off of one another for one community hiring opportunity.

chapters.summary: Won asks how OCH engages small businesses and MWBEs beyond current city vendors. G. Lee says OCH attends procurement fairs, educates MWBEs, and uses newsletters through agency partners and its own quarterly newsletter.
chapters.title: Chair asks about small businesses/MWBE outreach

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: How does OCH identify and engage small businesses in civic neighborhoods beyond vendors that are already

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: bidding on city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So our team has also been involved in a lot of vendor events like procurement fairs where we educate our MWBEs about the community hiring

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: program so that they understand how it works for city procurements that are subject to community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: Additionally, we've done newsletter outreach through our agency partners, and we also publish our own newsletter that goes out on a quarterly basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So we try different ways from different mediums to reach out to the public of vendors.

chapters.summary: Won asks whether OCH outreach has language access and what languages are available. G. Lee says English is currently primary, with plans to expand, and OCH leans on referral partners for other languages.
chapters.title: Chair asks language access

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Do you have language access in all of your efforts?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And if so, what languages are available for your outreach?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: Currently, English is the primary language.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Do you have plans to expand to other languages?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: And also, like, our referral partners also are equipped to provide other languages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So we lean heavily on our referral source partners and their agencies to support us there.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay, I hope you expand to at least five languages, not just leaning on the referrals.

chapters.summary: Won yields to Wong for a second round. Wong asks how a community hire is defined. G. Lee says it is defined by state law based on economic factors: low-income individuals and residents of low-income communities.
chapters.title: Chair yields to Wong; Wong asks definition of community hire

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it over to Councilmember Wong to ask a second round of questions.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can you define what exactly is a community hire?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like, do they live in the city or some other qualifications would qualify?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: positions as community hires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So community hire is defined under the state legislation that established community hiring, and it's based on economic factors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: So we look at two types of community hires, those who are low-income individuals and those living in low-income communities.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So do they have to live in New York City or are they going to live anywhere?

chapters.summary: Wong asks whether community hires must live in New York City. Harry says the definition is based on economic criteria under state law, though outreach is primarily targeted to New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Wong asks if community hires must live in NYC

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: They do, definitionally, it is based on economic criteria.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And again, that is rooted in state law.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: With that being said, the core work of talent and community hiring is to really connect more New Yorkers to jobs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so through our referral source partners, they are largely serving and

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: like I mentioned earlier, within all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so our outreach is primarily targeted towards New Yorkers and connecting it.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But because of the way that the state law is written, it is definitely economic criteria.

chapters.summary: Wong asks whether income baselines are state guidelines or set by OCH. G. Lee says they are based on federal poverty guidelines.
chapters.title: Wong asks about income baselines

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, but, okay, so the contractors, the vendors are definitely New York City-based.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But as a community hire, it's all like income-based rather than looking at where they live.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: As Michael, you mentioned, there are two different types of community hires.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So one of them is based on low-income zip codes, as well as NYCHA residents.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So NYCHA residents are the one population that is part of that residence-based community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: For the others, it is income-based.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And again, that's rooted in state law.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so it's not geographical.

chapters.summary: Wong asks what percentage of a vendor's jobs must be community hires. Harry says construction has a 30% hours goal, while other contracts have numerical goals based on contract value and hiring needs, not a fixed percentage.
chapters.title: Wong asks what percentage of jobs must be community hires

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Are the income...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Baselines based on state guidelines or something that your office determines?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - G. Lee
utterances.text: It's based on the federal poverty guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And, okay, so let's say a vendor is part of the community hire.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What percentage of their jobs have to be community hires?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So for the construction projects, those ones are the goal right now is 30% of the hours worked by community hires.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That's the goal.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: On the other side, it is not based on a percentage.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: The intention behind community hiring is to really drive these employers to the workforce system and make sure that they're working with the workforce system.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Ideally, we want them to be working with the workforce system for all of their jobs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: That's not exactly what's required.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: There's a specific numerical goal that will be attached to it based on the contract value.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But it's based on hiring needs, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so sometimes a vendor has to hire

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: no one to actually serve a contract and then they won't

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: but where they have vacancies, we want to make sure that they are working with the public workforce system for all of those if possible, but certainly at least the ones to meet their goals.

chapters.summary: Wong asks what incentive vendors have to participate in community hiring. Harry says vendors receiving city contracts have a responsibility to hire from the workforce system, and the city offers free workforce services and access to talent.
chapters.title: Wong asks incentive for vendors

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, maybe I'm confused of you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what is the incentive for becoming a vendor that's doing community hires?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Like, why bother?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So I think there's two things that I think are relevant here.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: One is we believe that there's a lot of city dollars that are being invested and that city vendors

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: have a responsibility to, if they're getting these contracts, right, and we're talking about the billions of dollars every year, we want those vendors to have an obligation to really...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Hire from the workforce system.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: In terms of an incentive, I think that's incumbent upon the city to really make sure that we are helping serve them, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so that's one of the things that certainly over time we want to work with the vendors to make sure that the city's workforce system is meeting their hiring needs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And if that means

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: that meeting their hiring needs and we can place someone today, great, fantastic, we want to do that.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: But that also may mean working with particular vendors or working with particular industries that have not historically worked with the public workforce system to help make sure that the city's workforce system are meeting those employers'needs.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: And so the incentive is we have a lot of talent here in New York City, and talent is not limited by...

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Factors of income, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So we want them to connect to that talent, and we want to connect the talent to these job opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: So the incentive of working with the public workforce system is that there's an enormous amount of talent that can fill the needs of these employers, and there are free services to these businesses, right?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: They don't have to pay to go and work with.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: The Workforce One centers.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Those are free services that are offered to those businesses to help fill their hiring needs.

chapters.summary: Won thanks Executive Directors Harry and Lee, says she looks forward to working with them, and moves to public testimony.
chapters.title: Chair closes Q&A and thanks witnesses

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much to Executive Director Lepari.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Lepari?

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Lepari.

utterances.speaker: Douglas Harry
utterances.text: Lepari.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Lepari.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And Executive Director Lee.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I look forward to working with both of you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Don't be so shy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: You're going to be here all the time.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: We're going to move on to panelists.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Won opens the floor for public testimony, reminds attendees of decorum rules, explains how to sign up, gives two minutes per speaker, and provides instructions for submitting written testimony.
chapters.title: Chair opens public testimony and gives instructions

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I now open the floor for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I remind the members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times other than when they're testifying.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And the witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recording as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms to wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And when recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's hearing topic on the Office of Community Hiring.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at councilnyc.gov or within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And I will now call the first panel.

chapters.summary: Won calls the first panel, Gregory Morris and Anthony DeCarl, and asks if anyone else wishes to testify.
chapters.title: Chair calls first panel of public witnesses

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And it is Gregory Morris and Anthony.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: the Carl.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And does anybody else wish to testify?

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Please let us know.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Welcome back.

chapters.summary: Greg Morris, CEO of the New York City Implementing Training Coalition, supports community hiring but says accountability and data are weak. He criticizes the $2,500 penalty as too small, calls for more NYC Talent staffing, and notes hiring halls served 20,000 people with only 2,000 conditional offers.
chapters.title: Greg Morris testifies on community hiring accountability and outreach

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: It's good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Thank you for making this time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: It's much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Madam Chair, it's nice to see you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Thank you for putting this conversation together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I'm Greg Morris, the CEO of the New York City Implementing Training Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I have testimony that's already been submitted, so I'm just going to share a couple of quick notes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: First and foremost,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: NYC ETC, the organization I represent, was actively engaged in support of community hiring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: We see it as an opportunity to use public spending to support folks from disadvantaged, economically disadvantaged communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: And I appreciate the way NYC Talent and the previous administration worked to try to maximize.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: The number of folks could fall into those categories.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: So I just want to start by saying it's the right opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I think where we see challenge, and that's sort of what I think you were poking at and probing here, is how it is that we actually can see whether or not it's making an impact, how it gets maximized across agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: As you noted, there's a number of agencies who don't participate in this, and that is also a strike against, I think, opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I also want to just add one or two other notes, and that is,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: is to say you also flagged what is the consequence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: And if we rewind the clock to the history with HireNYC, part of the reason why that didn't work is because folks weren't held accountable in a meaningful way for not following through on the expectations related to hiring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: And I think there's a concern here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: As you noted, the rules say you can hold an entity accountable for $2,500.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: What's the incentive for an entity to say, I must pay that because that's going to affect my bottom line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I just don't think we see that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: So I think this accountability conversation is particularly important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I wanted to note, too, related to community partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: The executive director talked about a number of organizations within the coalition who are community partners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: However, I just want to note NYC ETC, which represents 220 organizations, wants to see success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: And I think we can be an effective intermediary in trying to hold folks accountable to be able to meet these needs and expectation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: But that only happens, as one of the council members said, if there's active communication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: You also flagged the size and scope of NYC talent in managing this particular effort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: You highlighted that more staffing needs to be in place to be able to support that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I'd love to see NYC talent be resourced the way they need to be.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: They have vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: They have vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Do you want to come work there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: And not for nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Well, look, I got my hands full as it is right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: But not for nothing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Let's just put it this way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: If there are thousands of vendors that have these contracts and it's NYC Talent and the other agencies who have a responsibility for holding those vendors accountable, not just for communication and community partners for training and engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Otherwise, can the team of six, seven, eight be able to accomplish that as effectively as we would want?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: That's nothing against the individuals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: It's just about saying your budgets have to reflect that particular investment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Last but not least, I just want to note for you, as someone who has spent some time at the hiring halls recently,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: taking a look and seeing how things work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I just want you to be aware that I am appreciative and grateful for all the agency commitments that are made in supporting hiring halls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I do have this data and you've referenced it and you know it, but I just want to state it for the record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: The hiring hall model, the job fair model that the city put in motion served close to 20,000 individuals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: And we know of that, that was over the last year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: And of that 20,000, 2,000 had conditional offers made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: That should tell you there's a lot of people looking and it's not so easy to get hired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Job fairs and hiring halls aren't necessarily the answer, especially for individuals who come from backgrounds or haven't had access to opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: So I just want to note, like we missed that in some cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: And I would also suggest to you that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: the vendors that are being held accountable, they may need an adapter to be able to understand how it is that they can commit to, support, and ensure the success of individuals who live in the community that they might want to hire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I want to highlight that as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I think the coalition has a responsibility in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Last note for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: In terms of those hiring halls, and I think it counts here in this conversation, based on the data that we have for the last year of everybody who attended the hiring halls in the city, which presumably could be individuals from the communities we're talking about,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: more than half went to those hiring halls with a bachelor's degree or a master's degree in hand, which just leads me to the question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Is this model related to community hiring working to solve a problem of unemployment, underemployment, or just a transition to a better wage?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: Those are different things that we have to talk about in the job space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: I thank you, Chair, for bringing to the table the investment in workforce development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Greg Morris
utterances.text: This administration as it currently exists has not clarified how it will continue to elevate workforce development and instead has been filling potholes along the way.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Gregory.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And as always, if you have ideas for legislation to codify any of the things that we have to push for, I think we're going to have to advocate for them to expand their office because as you heard directly from the executive directors, they did not seem to

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: feel the need to hire any additional staff from what they have.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: And I believe

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: I believe right behind you is Anthony DeCarl.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Julie Won
utterances.text: You can come up and testify.

chapters.summary: Anthony DeCarlos, a former hospitality worker, testifies about New York Labor Law Section 210B, which takes effect November 8 and gives workers the right to see personnel files. He asks the committee to make this right part of the community hiring pipeline so workers can correct records before they affect employment.
chapters.title: Anthony DeCarlos testifies on personnel file rights and community hiring

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to be reading from my phone, just to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Juan and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: My name is Anthony DeCarlos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: I'm a former hospitality worker, 10 plus years in New York City restaurant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: I run Clear the Records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: It's a free education site that teaches hospitality and gig workers to check and dispute the records employers report about them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: I'm here about a right that takes effect 12 days from now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: On November 8th, New York Labor Law Section 210B gives every worker in the state the right to see their own personnel files.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: A worker can demand it in writing, and an employer must hand over a free copy within five business days, twice a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: If something negative goes into the file, the worker must be told within 10 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: The worker's written response becomes a part of the file, and it travels with them wherever the record is sent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: It applies even when the background check vendor holds the records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: what this law is worth because I've lived the version without it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: When I lost my job, my unemployment was held up for months by the employer that said that there was misconduct

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: for my work history to the Department of Labor, which later withdrew the misconduct report from my record in June of this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: My wages were reported under the wrong company and the wrong subsidiary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: Every error was invisible to me until it cost me money and work to find out what was happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: Community hiring cannot place workers whose files are wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: Until November 8th, workers could not even look at them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: So my simple ask is, as this committee oversees the Office of Community Hiring, make Section 210B part of the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: Every worker who walks into a city program should walk out knowing they can demand their files before a database decides their future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: To harm them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: A right workers don't know about deserve to be hired anyway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony DeCarlos
utterances.text: Thank you.

summary: The Committee on Workforce Development held an oversight hearing on the Office of Community Hiring, chaired by Julie Won.
NYC Talent and OCH testified on program rollout, contract goals, hiring data, staffing, and accountability, facing questions from Council Members Won, Epstein, and Wong.
Public witnesses Greg Morris and Anthony DeCarlos testified on accountability gaps and new personnel file rights under Labor Law Section 210B.
